Rules (subset):
RULE 1: For base ISAs with XLEN ≥ 64, the RDCYCLE pseudoinstruction reads the full 64-bit value of the cycle CSR.
RULE 2: The cycle counter can be read using the canonical csrrs rd, cycle, x0 instruction as well as the read-only CSRRC, CSRRSI, and CSRRCI forms.
RULE 3: The RDCYCLE pseudoinstruction reads the low XLEN bits of the cycle CSR.
RULE 4: The presented code sequence ensures that a consistent 64-bit cycle counter value is read even if the lower half overflows between the reads.
RULE 5: The cycle CSR is located at address 0xC00 and is designated as unprivileged read-only (URO).
RULE 6: The cycleh CSR is located at address 0xC80 and is designated as unprivileged read-only (URO).
RULE 7: The cycle CSR provides a cycle counter that is accessed by the RDCYCLE instruction.
RULE 8: When the RDCYCLE instruction reads CSR 0xC00, the value returned equals the current cycle counter.
RULE 9: The mcycle register is located at address 0xB00 and provides the Machine cycle counter.
RULE 10: The mcycle CSR counts the number of clock cycles executed by the processor core on which the hart is running.
RULE 11: A write to the mcycle CSR stores the specified value into the register.
RULE 12: A write to the mcycle CSR takes effect after the writing instruction has otherwise completed.
RULE 13: If the mcycle CSR is shared between harts on the same core, writes to the mcycle CSR are visible to all those harts.
RULE 14: The cycle counter continues to increment regardless of any reads or writes to the mcounteren register.
RULE 15: When the CY bit in mcounteren is clear, attempts to read the cycle CSR while executing in S-mode or U-mode cause an illegal-instruction exception.
RULE 16: When the CY bit in mcounteren is set, access to the cycle CSR is permitted in the next implemented privilege mode (S-mode if implemented, otherwise U-mode).
RULE 17: The cycle CSR is a read-only shadow of the mcycle register.
RULE 18: If a hart that supports U‑mode writes any value to the CY field of the mcounteren CSR, then the write does not raise an illegal‑instruction exception and a subsequent read of mcounteren.CY returns either the value written or zero.

RULE 20: When the CY bit in the mcountinhibit register is clear, the mcycle CSR increments on each cycle.
RULE 21: When the CY bit in the mcountinhibit register is set, the mcycle CSR does not increment on any cycle.
RULE 22: When the mcycle CSR is shared between harts on the same core, the mcountinhibit.CY field is also shared, and writes to mcountinhibit.CY are visible to those harts, thereby controlling whether the shared mcycle CSR increments on each cycle.
RULE 23: By default the cycle counter is not filtered by privilege mode.
RULE 24: The privilege-mode filtering applied to the cycle counter is the same as that applied to the instret counter.
RULE 25: Bit 62 of mcyclecfg, named MINH, when set inhibits counting of cycle events while the processor is executing in machine mode.
RULE 26: Bit 61 of mcyclecfg, named SINH, when set inhibits counting of cycle events while the processor is executing in supervisor or hypervisor mode.
RULE 27: Bit 60 of mcyclecfg, named UINH, when set inhibits counting of cycle events while the processor is executing in user mode.
RULE 28: If all INH bits (MINH, SINH, UINH, VSINH, VUINH) in mcyclecfg are zero, counting of cycle events is enabled in all privilege modes.
RULE 29: For any INH bit in positions 61 through 58 of mcyclecfg, if the associated privilege mode is not implemented, that bit is read-only zero.
RULE 30: The cycle counter will increment for each CPU cycle while the CPU is executing in a non-inhibited privilege mode.
RULE 31: When mcounteren[0] = 1 and menvcfg.CDE = 1, the cycle register may be read or written via the indirect CSRs while siselect = 0x40.
RULE 32: If mcounteren[0] = 0, any access to the cycle register, cycleh, cyclecfg, or cyclecfgh via the indirect CSRs raises an illegal-instruction exception.

RULE 34: If the difference between successive reads of the elapsed cycle counter (CtrCycleCounter) does not equal the difference between successive reads of the mcycle CSR, then the counters are not incrementing at the same rate.
RULE 35: Only cycles while CTR is active are counted, where active implies that the current privilege mode is enabled for recording and CTR is not frozen.
RULE 36: Unimplemented CCE bits, which are part of the cycle count exponent, are read-only 0.
RULE 37: If a CSR write to the cycle counter using the standard counter‑modification mechanism does not change the cycle CSR’s readback value (or raises an illegal‑instruction exception), then the implementation violates the rule.
RULE 38: If the CY bit in scounteren is clear, a read of the cycle register while executing in U-mode causes an illegal-instruction exception.
RULE 39: If the CY bit in scounteren is set, access to the cycle register from U-mode is permitted.
RULE 40: If the CY bit in scounteren is read-only zero, a U-mode read of the cycle register causes an illegal-instruction exception.
RULE 41: The writability of the CY bit in scounteren is not affected by the setting of the CY bit in mcounteren.
RULE 42: A U-mode read of the cycle register causes an illegal-instruction exception unless both the CY bit in scounteren and the CY bit in mcounteren are set.
RULE 43: If both the CY bit in scounteren and the CY bit in mcounteren are set, a U-mode read of the cycle register is permitted.
RULE 44: When the 64-bit cycle counter wraps, the mcause or scause register is set to exception code 13 (counter-overflow interrupt).
RULE 45: When XLEN>32, any attempt to access a high-half cycle CSR (e.g., cycleh) raises an illegal-instruction exception.
RULE 46: In M-mode, accessing cycle register should result in no exception (# Result: mcause = 0x0) [# Extension Must Be Active: NONE; csrr a0, 0xc00; # Result: mcause = 0x0].
RULE 47: In S-mode, accessing cycle register should result in illegal-instruction exception (# Result: mcause = 0x2) [# Extension Must Be Active: NONE; call machine_to_supervisor; csrr a0, 0xc00; # Result: mcause = 0x2].
RULE 48: In U-mode, accessing cycle register should result in illegal-instruction exception (# Result: mcause = 0x2) [# Extension Must Be Active: NONE; call machine_to_user; csrr a0, 0xc00; # Result: mcause = 0x2].

RESPONSE:
=========
============================================================
The cycle CSR (address 0xC00) is an unprivileged read‑only shadow of the machine‑mode mcycle register that returns the current processor cycle count, with the RDCYCLE pseudoinstruction delivering the full XLEN‑wide value on XLEN ≥ 64 systems. The counter increments each CPU cycle unless inhibited by the CY bit in mcountinhibit or by the appropriate INH bits in mcyclecfg, and it continues counting irrespective of mcounteren settings. Reads are always permitted in M‑mode; in S‑ and U‑mode they are allowed only when the CY field of mcounteren (and, for U‑mode, also scounteren) is set, otherwise an illegal‑instruction exception is raised. A 64‑bit wrap generates exception code 13, and any write to the cycle CSR must be ignored and must not alter its value.

RESPONSE:
=========
============================================================
The fcsr is a per‑hart control‑status register that combines the floating‑point rounding‑mode field (frm) and the accrued‑exception‑flags field (fflags) used by floating‑point instructions. Both sub‑fields are readable and writable from any privilege level (URW), are invisible to other harts, and accesses never generate a trap regardless of which extensions are implemented. The rounding‑mode field supplies the dynamic rounding mode for operations that request it, while the flag field records any floating‑point exceptions that have occurred since software last cleared them; these flags do not cause traps. Modifications to the FS state do not affect the stored fcsr contents, and reserved bits are ignored or read as zero.

The fflags CSR records the five accrued floating‑point exception flags (Invalid, Divide‑by‑Zero, Overflow, Underflow, Inexact) that are set by any FP arithmetic instruction that encounters the corresponding condition and remain set until software clears them. It is part of the fcsr register but can be accessed directly with unprivileged read/write permissions, and reads or writes in any privilege mode generate no trap. The FRFLAGS instruction copies the current flag bits into an integer register, while FSFLAGS can read the flags and write a new value using the low bits of a source register, with writes updating only the five flag bits. Flag writes never cause traps, and writes larger than five bits are masked to the flag field; changing the FS field or disabling FP does not alter the stored flags.

Rules (subset):

RULE 14: If the frm field of a floating‑point instruction is 101, 110, or 111, then the instruction raises an illegal‑instruction exception (mcause set to the illegal‑instruction code).
RULE 15: When the rm field of a scalar floating-point instruction is encoded as DYN (binary 111), the instruction uses the rounding mode specified in the frm CSR.
RULE 16: The sum is rounded according to the frm register.

RULE 18: The rtz variants vfcvt.rtz.xu.f.v and vfcvt.rtz.x.f.v do not use the rounding mode in the frm register and instead round towards zero.
RULE 19: The frm register has privilege level URW (User-Read/Write).

The frm register holds the current dynamic floating‑point rounding mode as a 3‑bit field that selects RNE, RTZ, RDN, RUP, or RMM, with encodings 101‑111 causing an illegal‑instruction exception when interpreted as a rounding mode. It is accessed through the fcsr CSR (bits 7‑5) and by the FRRM and FSRM instructions, which transfer the 3‑bit value between integer registers and frm. The register is user‑read/write (URW) and can be read or written without exception in U‑, S‑, or M‑mode, even when the F, V, or related extensions are enabled. Writes are masked to the low three bits, so writing larger values does not set illegal patterns in the stored field.

The hip CSR holds the set of pending hypervisor‑mode interrupts and is defined with HRW (read/write) access. hpmcounter10 is a read‑only shadow of the 64‑bit machine performance‑monitoring counter mhpmcounter10 that reports events selected by the corresponding mhpmevent10 register. Its overflow status (OF) bit, controlled via mhpmevent10, is set on counter wrap‑around and triggers the standard count‑overflow interrupt (LCOFIP/LCOFIE) unless the OF bit is already set; the same mhpmevent10 bits also inhibit counting in specified privilege modes. When the unsigned counter wraps, the OF flag in mhpmevent8 is set and, if the flag was previously clear, a count‑overflow interrupt is generated, reflected in the LCOFIP pending bit and controlled by the LCOFIE enable bits and possible delegation via mideleg. A CSR write to hpmcounter8 takes effect after the writing instruction completes, and after an overflow the counter and its OF flag must be cleared before another overflow interrupt can be generated.

The mcause CSR records the cause of the most recent trap, encoding an interrupt flag (the most‑significant bit) and a numeric cause code that identifies the specific exception or interrupt. It is an MXLEN‑bit machine‑mode read/write register; accesses from S‑ or U‑mode raise an illegal‑instruction exception, while software may write it explicitly but hardware writes only when a trap is taken into M‑mode. Hardware updates mcause only on traps taken into M‑mode, writing the appropriate flag and code according to the prioritized exception table, and does not write it when the trap is delegated to S‑mode, when a double‑trap occurs (setting code 16), or when extensions such as Smrnmi suppress the update. On reset the register reads 0, and the MSB distinguishes interrupts (1) from exceptions (0), with defined codes covering software, timer, external, page‑fault, and other standard causes; reserved or undefined codes are reported unchanged.

The mconfigptr CSR is a mandatory machine‑mode read‑only register that holds the physical address of the system configuration data structure. Its value is MXLEN‑wide and the low log₂ (n) bits are forced to zero to satisfy the required alignment (MXLEN = 8·n). Reads are allowed only in M‑mode without exception, while any access from S‑ or U‑mode or any write attempt from any privilege level raises an illegal‑instruction exception and leaves the register unchanged. Consequently, writes—including attempts to set the least‑significant address bit—never affect the value returned on readback.

The mcounteren CSR is a machine‑mode register that controls which hardware performance counters (cycle, time, instruction‑retired, and the HPM counters) are readable by the next‑lower privilege level. It contains a CY bit for the cycle counter, TM for the time counter, IR for the instruction‑retired counter, and a set of HPM bits; setting a bit grants read access to that counter in S‑mode (or U‑mode if S is not implemented), while a cleared bit causes any read from the lower mode to raise an illegal‑instruction exception. Access to mcounteren itself is restricted to M‑mode—any attempt to read or write it from S‑ or U‑mode triggers an illegal‑instruction exception, and M‑mode accesses never fault regardless of extensions. The register’s bits are advisory only: reading or writing mcounteren does not affect the counters, and the bits reliably round‑trip on read‑back.

mhpmcounter4 is a machine‑level 64‑bit hardware performance counter whose increment source is selected by the WARL CSR mhpmevent4. The counter is readable in M‑mode and via the read‑only shadow hpmcounter4 in lower modes, but reads in S‑ or U‑mode cause an illegal‑instruction exception unless the HPM4 bit in mcounteren is set, while writes are permitted only in M‑mode and take effect after the writing instruction completes. The mimpid CSR provides a machine‑mode read‑only identifier that must be present in every RISC‑V implementation. It can be read without fault only while executing in M‑mode; attempts to read it from S‑ or U‑mode raise an illegal‑instruction exception (mcause 0x2). The minstret CSR (address 0xB02) holds the lower 32 bits of the machine‑mode instruction‑retired counter and can be written, with the new value taking effect after the writing instruction completes. Access to minstret is unrestricted in M‑mode (no exception regardless of extensions) but illegal in S‑ or U‑mode unless the IR bit in mcounteren permits reading the instret shadow CSR; writes are not permitted outside M‑mode.

mstateen0 is a machine‑mode read/write CSR that governs the visibility of architectural state to less‑privileged modes. Its principal fields—SE0, ENVCFG, CSRIND and groups such as CTR, FCSR, etc.—enable access to the corresponding hstateen0/sstateen0 CSRs, environment‑configuration CSRs, CSR indirection, and specific state components; any unimplemented or reserved bits read as zero and are not writable, and all writable bits are cleared to zero on reset. The register can be accessed only in M‑mode; reads or writes in S‑ or U‑mode raise an illegal‑instruction exception, and any zero bit in mstateen0 forces the matching bit in hstateen0 and sstateen0 to be read‑only zero. When a lower‑privilege mode attempts to use state whose enable bit is zero (e.g., the CTR group), an illegal‑instruction exception is generated, and raising such an exception in M‑mode while the C bit is set but no custom state is accessed indicates non‑conforming hardware.

RULE 35: Instruction address-translation and protection are unaffected by the setting of the MPRV bit in mstatus.
RULE 36: An MRET or SRET instruction that changes the privilege mode to a mode less privileged than M also sets the MPRV bit in mstatus to 0.
RULE 37: When the MXR bit in mstatus is 0, only loads from pages marked readable (R=1) will succeed.
RULE 38: When the MXR bit in mstatus is 1, loads from pages marked either readable or executable (R=1 or X=1) will succeed.
RULE 39: When the SUM bit in mstatus is 0, S-mode memory accesses to pages that are accessible by U-mode (U=1) will fault.
RULE 40: SUM in mstatus has no effect when page-based virtual memory is not in effect.
RULE 41: SUM in mstatus is ordinarily ignored when not executing in S-mode, but it is in effect when MPRV=1 and MPP=S.
RULE 42: The SUM mechanisms encoded in mstatus have no impact on whether access-fault exceptions are raised due to PMP.
RULE 43: The MBE, SBE, and UBE bits are fields in mstatus and mstatush that control the endianness of memory accesses other than instruction fetches.
RULE 44: Instruction fetches are always little-endian and are not affected by the mstatus MBE, SBE, or UBE bits.
RULE 45: The mstatus.MBE bit controls the endianness of non-instruction-fetch memory accesses made from M-mode when mstatus.MPRV = 0.
RULE 46: When mstatus.MBE = 0, non-instruction-fetch memory accesses from M-mode are little-endian.
RULE 47: When mstatus.MBE = 1, non-instruction-fetch memory accesses from M-mode are big-endian.
RULE 48: The mstatus.SBE bit controls the endianness of explicit load and store memory accesses made from S-mode.
RULE 49: When mstatus.SBE = 0, explicit load and store memory accesses from S-mode are little-endian.
RULE 50: When mstatus.SBE = 1, explicit load and store memory accesses from S-mode are big-endian.
RULE 51: The mstatus.UBE bit controls the endianness of explicit load and store memory accesses made from U-mode.
RULE 52: When mstatus.UBE = 0, explicit load and store memory accesses from U-mode are little-endian.
RULE 53: When mstatus.UBE = 1, explicit load and store memory accesses from U-mode are big-endian.
RULE 54: When the TVM bit in mstatus is 1, attempts to read the satp CSR while executing in S-mode raise an illegal-instruction exception.
RULE 55: When the TVM bit in mstatus is 1, attempts to write the satp CSR while executing in S-mode raise an illegal-instruction exception.
RULE 56: When the TVM bit in mstatus is 1, attempts to execute an SFENCE.VMA instruction while executing in S-mode raise an illegal-instruction exception.
RULE 57: When the TVM bit in mstatus is 0, attempts to read or write the satp CSR while executing in S-mode are permitted.
RULE 58: When the TVM bit in mstatus is 0, attempts to execute an SFENCE.VMA instruction while executing in S-mode are permitted.
RULE 59: When the TVM bit in mstatus is 0, attempts to execute a SINVAL.VMA instruction while executing in S-mode are permitted.
RULE 60: The TW field in mstatus is a WARL field.
RULE 61: The TSR field in mstatus is a WARL field.
RULE 62: When the TSR bit in mstatus is 1, attempts to execute SRET while executing in S-mode raise an illegal-instruction exception.
RULE 63: When the TSR bit in mstatus is 0, attempts to execute SRET while executing in S-mode are permitted.
RULE 64: The mstatus register contains the FS[1:0] and VS[1:0] fields, which are WARL fields, and the XS[1:0] field, which is a read-only field.
RULE 65: The SD bit in mstatus is a read-only bit that summarizes whether either the FS, VS, or XS fields signal the presence of dirty state that will require saving extended user context to memory.
RULE 66: If the FS, VS, and XS fields in mstatus are all read-only zero, then the SD bit in mstatus is also always zero.
RULE 67: If the F extension is implemented, the FS field in mstatus shall not be read-only zero.
RULE 68: In harts without additional user extensions requiring new state, the XS field in mstatus is read-only zero.
RULE 69: Changing the setting of the FS field in mstatus has no effect on the contents of the floating-point register state.
RULE 70: Setting the FS field in mstatus to Off does not destroy the floating-point state, and setting the FS field to Initial does not clear the floating-point contents.
RULE 71: The FS field in mstatus is set directly by privileged code when resuming a user context, while the XS field in mstatus is set indirectly by writing to the status register of the individual extensions.
RULE 72: Machine mode and Supervisor mode share a single copy of the FS, VS, and XS bits in mstatus.
RULE 73: The SD bit in mstatus is read-only and is set when either the FS, VS, or XS bits in mstatus encode a Dirty state (i.e., SD = (FS==0b11 OR VS==0b11 OR XS==0b11)).
RULE 74: In mstatus, the encoding 0 for FS and VS means Off, 1 means Initial, 2 means Clean, and 3 means Dirty.
RULE 75: If the XS field in mstatus reads 0, then all extension states are off; if it reads 1, then no extensions are dirty and at least one extension is on; if it reads 2, then no extensions are dirty and at least one extension is clean; if it reads 3, then at least one extension is dirty.
RULE 76: When an extension's status field in mstatus is set to Off, any instruction that attempts to read or write the corresponding state causes an illegal-instruction exception.
RULE 77: If the FS, VS, or XS field in mstatus is Off, executing an instruction that reads the corresponding state causes an exception.
RULE 78: If the FS, VS, or XS field in mstatus is Off, executing an instruction that may modify the corresponding state causes an exception.

RULE 81: If the FS, VS, or XS field in mstatus is Dirty, executing an instruction that may modify the corresponding state leaves the field in the Dirty state.

RESPONSE:
=========
============================================================
The mstatus CSR holds the machine‑level status of the hart, including global interrupt‑enable bits, privilege‑mode fields for trap entry/return, extension‑state fields (FS, VS, XS) that track whether floating‑point, vector, or other user extensions are off, clean, initial or dirty, and a read‑only SD bit that summarises any dirty extension state. It also contains control bits for memory‑management and virtualisation (MPP, MPIE, SPP, SPIE, MPRV, MXR, SUM, TVM, TSR, TW) and endianness selectors (MBE, SBE, UBE). The register is machine‑read/write only; any access from lower privilege levels raises an illegal‑instruction exception, writes are masked to XLEN and only architecturally defined fields are retained, while read‑only or WARL fields ignore writes to undefined bits. Illegal‑instruction exceptions are also generated when VS=Off for vector operations, FS=Off for floating‑point operations, or when TVM, TSR, or TW are set and privileged instructions such as satp access, SFENCE.VMA, SRET, or WFI are attempted in disallowed modes.

The mtval CSR supplies trap‑specific information to software, typically the faulting virtual address or, for illegal‑instruction and certain fetch faults, the offending instruction bits, and it is written by hardware when a trap is taken into M‑mode. The mtvec CSR (address 0x305) holds the machine‑mode trap‑vector base address (BASE) and a mode selector (MODE) that controls PC redirection on traps. BASE must be 4‑byte aligned (low two bits are zeroed when used as an address); MODE = 0 (Direct) sends all machine‑mode traps to BASE, while MODE = 1 (Vectored) sends synchronous exceptions to BASE and the timer interrupt (cause 2) to BASE + 4 × cause + 4. mtvec is readable and writable only in M‑mode; attempts to access it from S‑ or U‑mode raise an illegal‑instruction exception (mcause 0x2). Writes with unsupported MODE values, misaligned BASE, or out‑of‑range bits are silently corrected or masked so that subsequent reads return a legal, aligned BASE and a valid MODE (typically 0) without raising an exception.

pmpcfg10 is the configuration register for PMP entry 10, specifying the address‑matching mode (A), lock bit (L), and the read/write/execute (R,W,X) permission fields that together determine region access for Machine, Supervisor and User modes, especially when MML is set. pmpcfg6 is the PMP configuration register for entry 6, governing read, write, and instruction‑fetch permissions (R, W, X bits) and selecting the address‑matching mode via the A field (OFF, TOR, NA4, NAPOT). The entry is disabled when A = 0; TOR mode uses adjacent pmpaddr registers to define a range, while NA4 and NAPOT modes define fixed‑size ranges based on the pmpaddr pattern, and the G bit determines how the lower bits of the pmpaddr are masked on read. Access to pmpcfg6 is permitted only in machine mode—any read or write from supervisor or user mode raises an illegal‑instruction exception, and a write that sets R = 0 and W = 1 also raises an illegal‑instruction exception. Writes to the configuration fields are not reflected on subsequent reads (the register appears read‑only), and no exception is generated for such writes even when the P or Smepmp extensions are enabled.

The senvcfg CSR defines the user‑mode execution environment, exposing fields that enable or disable cache‑block operations (CBIE, CBCFE, CBZE), pointer‑masking mode (PMM), and extensions such as Zicfiss (SSE) and Zicfilp (LPE). The SSE bit activates the Zicfiss extension and shadow‑stack control‑flow protection, while PMM selects pointer‑masking granularity (disabled, XLEN‑57, or XLEN‑48); when SSE is cleared the field is read‑only zero and related 16‑bit instructions revert to Zcmop behavior. Access to senvcfg is SRW‑privileged: M‑mode may read/write freely, whereas S‑ and U‑mode accesses generate illegal‑instruction traps unless the ENVCFG bits in the appropriate state‑enable CSR permit it, and writes are reflected on subsequent reads with undefined bits masked out.

The sepc CSR holds the virtual address of the instruction that caused a trap and is used by the SRET instruction to resume execution after returning from S‑mode. It is an SXLEN‑wide read/write register with Supervisor Read/Write privilege, accessible without exception in M‑mode and S‑mode but causing an illegal‑instruction fault in U‑mode. Hardware writes sepc on every trap taken to S‑mode (including delegated, double‑trap, and HS‑mode entries) with the faulting or interrupted instruction address, while software may also write it explicitly; the low bit is always zero and, when IALIGN = 32, the next low bit is masked on reads (though it can still be written). The register is WARL, constrained to hold any valid virtual address, and it is modified only by trap entry or explicit software writes.

On traps delegated to S‑mode or taken into HS‑mode the hardware writes stval with the faulting virtual address (or zero) for breakpoint, misaligned, access‑fault, page‑fault, hardware‑error, and illegal‑instruction exceptions, and with the software‑check cause for software‑check traps; otherwise it is never written automatically. The vsepc CSR holds the virtual supervisor exception program counter and is readable and writable only in hypervisor mode (HRW), while accesses in M‑mode succeed silently and accesses in U‑mode raise an illegal‑instruction exception. Accesses are legal when the H extension is active and generate no exception.

The vsie CSR is the virtual supervisor‑mode interrupt‑enable register, holding enable bits for the standard supervisor interrupt types (SEI, STI, SSI, LCOFI) in a virtualized context. Its fields include these enable bits plus reserved/WPRI bits, all of which retain the written XLEN‑wide value on read (with any bits above XLEN masked off) while bits for unimplemented interrupt types read as zero. The register can be accessed without exception in machine and supervisor modes, but generates an illegal‑instruction exception in user mode, and this access behavior is unchanged by the presence of extensions such as H, Shlcofideleg, Smaia, Smcdeleg, Ssaia, or Sscofpmf. The vsie bits are consulted together with sip/hip and hideleg to decide virtual interrupt delivery to higher privilege modes, and writes of values larger than the XLEN are simply masked rather than causing undefined all‑ones results.

The vstart CSR (address 0x008) holds the architectural index of the vector element at which a trapped vector instruction should resume; hardware writes it on a trap, software can read or write it, and it is automatically cleared to zero at the start of every vector instruction (including vsetvl). It is a URW register accessible in M‑, S‑ and U‑mode unless the VS field is disabled, in which case any access causes an illegal‑instruction exception, and writes are masked to the implemented field width. Many vector operations that cannot safely restart with a non‑zero index (e.g., reductions, mask‑logical, vmsbf/vmsif/vmsof, and most crypto instructions) raise an illegal‑instruction exception when vstart ≠ 0 or when its value is not a required multiple of the element‑group size. When a trap occurs, vstart records the faulting element index, and precise‑trap semantics require that only elements with index ≥ vstart may be modified, matching the effect of restarting the instruction at that index.
